n: The fateful day arrives — the thirteenth of Adar, nearly a year after Haman’s decree. The day enemies hoped to destroy the Jews is “turned to the contrary.” Reversal is the great theme of Esther.

f.w: it was turned to the contrary
f.g: Turned upside down — the key idea of the whole book.

n: Jews throughout the empire band together to defend themselves against those who attack them. No one can stand against them.

f.g: Those who tried to harm them — the fighting was defensive.

n: Persian officials side with the Jews, out of respect and fear of Mordecai’s new power.
Mordecai’s influence keeps growing throughout the empire.
The Jews defeat those who hated them and came against them. The text is blunt; it reflects a life-or-death battle in an ancient world, not a model for personal revenge.
In the citadel of Susa itself, five hundred attackers are killed.

f.g: The fortified royal district of Susa.

n: The names of Haman’s ten sons begin. In Hebrew scrolls of Esther, these names are traditionally written in a special column, like a list.

f.g: A Persian name, like all of Haman’s sons’ names.

n: Three more of Haman’s sons are named.

f.g: Persian name; its meaning is uncertain.

n: The last four sons. Many of these names have Persian roots, showing Haman’s family was well established at court.

f.g: The tenth and last son named.

n: Haman’s ten sons are killed. Notably, the Jews take no plunder, though the decree allowed it — unlike Saul, who took Amalekite spoil long before. They fought to survive, not to get rich.

f.w: on the spoil laid they not their hand

n: The death toll in Susa is reported to the king that same day.
The king tells Esther the news and wonders how things went elsewhere. Then he again asks what more she wants.
Esther asks for one more day of self-defense in Susa, where enemies apparently remained, and for the bodies of Haman’s sons to be publicly displayed as a warning.

f.w: let Haman's ten sons be hanged
f.g: Their bodies, already dead, were displayed publicly as a deterrent.

n: The king agrees, and the order is carried out.
On the fourteenth, Jews in Susa defend themselves again, killing 300 attackers, and again taking no plunder.

f.w: on the prey they laid not their hand

n: Across the empire, Jews defend themselves and gain rest from their enemies, killing 75,000 attackers. Once more, the text stresses that they took no plunder.
In the provinces the fighting is on the thirteenth, and they rest and celebrate on the fourteenth.

f.w: made it a day of feasting and gladness
f.g: The origin of the feast of Purim.

n: In Susa the fighting lasted two days, so the Jews there celebrated on the fifteenth. This explains why Purim falls on two different dates.

f.w: on the fifteenth day of the same they rested
f.g: Still today, walled cities like Jerusalem celebrate “Shushan Purim” on the 15th of Adar.

n: So village Jews celebrated on the fourteenth with feasting and sending gifts of food to one another — a custom still practiced at Purim.

f.g: Gifts of food, still exchanged at Purim today.

n: Mordecai writes to Jews near and far to record what happened.
He establishes an annual two-day celebration on the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar.
These days remember when sorrow turned to joy and mourning to celebration. They are to include feasting, gifts to friends, and gifts to the poor — joy that reaches out to others.
The Jews accept Mordecai’s instructions and continue the celebration they had begun.
A summary of the story: Haman, enemy of all the Jews, plotted to destroy them and cast Pur (the lot) to choose the day.
But when the matter came before the king, Haman’s evil plan turned back on his own head.

f.w: should return upon his own head

n: The feast is named Purim, from “Pur,” the lot Haman cast. The name itself is a reminder that what seemed like chance was overruled by God.
The Jews commit themselves, their children, and any who join them to keep these two days every year without fail.

f.w: took upon them, and upon their seed
all such as joined themselves unto them

n: Purim is to be remembered in every generation, family, province, and city. Remembering God’s deliverances helps faith endure.

f.w: remembered and kept throughout every generation

n: Queen Esther, with Mordecai, writes with full authority to confirm the festival. Esther, once hidden, now speaks with royal authority for her people.
The letters go to all 127 provinces with “words of peace and truth” — a greeting of well-being and faithfulness.
The letters confirm the dates of Purim, along with remembrance of the fasting and lamenting that preceded the deliverance. Today a fast, the “Fast of Esther,” comes the day before Purim.

f.w: the matters of the fastings and their cry

n: Esther’s decree makes these rules official, and they are written down in the records. Her leadership closes the story of Purim.

f.w: it was written in the book
f.g: Recorded in an official book, perhaps the royal or community records.
